## 0. Scope and boundaries
VOL-C specifies the **coordination service's own surface**: the tools the invocation service exposes to agent sessions (messaging, work-log), the four ingress doors, reply/group/fan-out semantics, the NEW/REUSE event→session mapping, scheduler admission and the complete send state machine, and the enforceable authorization model.
**Hermes-owned, referenced not rebuilt** (verified against https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/api-server, fetched 2026-11-08):
| Hermes capability | Contract this spec relies on | |---|---| | Session continuation | `POST /v1/chat/completions` with `X-Hermes-Session-Id: <id>` (existing session = next turn); a request with no continuation id starts a fresh session | | Session key scope | `X-Hermes-Session-Key` header (max 256 chars, no `\r\n\x00`, echoed back; advertised via `/v1/capabilities` `session_key_header`) — feeds the memory provider's stable scope | | Durable admission | `Idempotency-Key` header on `POST /v1/chat/completions`, `/v1/responses`, `/v1/runs`: first request runs once; exact retry replays; changed payload → `409 admission_conflict` | | Runs API | `POST /v1/runs` returns `run_id`; `GET /v1/runs/{id}`, `/events`; `session_id` surfaced in run status; session turn leases serialize concurrent writers | | Sessions REST | `POST /api/sessions` (create), `GET /api/sessions/{id}`, `DELETE /api/sessions/{id}` (deleted ids are never reused; tombstones) | | Failure codes | `409 admission_conflict`, `409 unknown_execution`, `503 runtime_draining`/`storage_unavailable` with `Retry-After` | | Session resume | Scheduler orphan-scan re-queue (DESIGN FACT-29) |
VOL-C does **not** define: record schemas (VOL-A / DATA-MODEL), acceptance and report-verification semantics (VOL-D / F-013), bridge lifecycle (F-014–F-017), or the scheduler's own algorithms (existing code).

## 1. Principals and credentials (F-012 foundation)

### 1.1 Principal classes
Every call to any service surface authenticates to exactly one principal class. The class is derived from the **credential**, never from a request field.
| Class | Credential | Issued by | Lives in | |---|---|---|---| | `vp` | VP token | operator provisioning | token file/dir named in service config | | `scheduler` | scheduler callback credential | operator provisioning | shared only by scheduler ↔ service | | `agent:<agent-id>` | per-agent service token | operator provisioning, one per configured agent | `token_dir` (pattern of DATA-MODEL/FACT-20) | | `service` | the invocation service's own credential (DuckBrain write + scheduler mutation) | operator provisioning | held by the service process only |
- **VOLC-001** A request's principal class and id are established solely by its credential. `from`, `as`, or body identity fields are **attribution data, not authentication**: a mismatch between credential identity and body identity is refused `403 identity_mismatch` and audited. - **VOLC-002** Gateway credentials (`gateways[].auth_token_ref`, used by the service to reach Hermes gateways) and **agent-to-service credentials** (agent tokens used by sessions to call service tools) are distinct credential populations. No agent token is accepted at a gateway, and no gateway credential is accepted at the service ingress. - **VOLC-003** Credentials are referenced by config (`auth_token_ref` / `token_dir`), never inlined. The service loads them at startup and on rotation signal; expiry and revocation are operator actions on the referenced file/store: the service re-validates the credential against the loaded set on every call, reloading on file change or `POST /v1/admin/reload-credentials` from a `vp` or `scheduler` principal. This is CREDENTIAL revocation. Permission revocation is a different mechanism and never uses this path: it is session-scoped per VOL-A-043 and §8.9 (snapshot), with the single per-page exception in §8.8 VOLC-072b. A revoked credential fails `401` with zero side effects. - **VOLC-004** No hierarchy agent ever holds the scheduler's mutating credential, the service's own DuckBrain write credential, or a gateway auth token (DESIGN §6.1). Violation detection (a token presented for the wrong class) is an integrity violation: refused, audited, counted.

### 1.2 Two credential planes, one diagram
``` agents --(agent service tokens)--> SERVICE TOOLS --(service credential)--> DuckBrain agents <--(gateway token, service-held)--- Hermes gateways <--(scheduler callback cred)-- scheduler ```
The service is the **only** writer of `/chd/*` keys. See §2.1.

## 2. The agent-facing service tools (D-014, F-008, F-018)

### 2.1 Write-path decision: agent → service → DuckBrain
DESIGN CT-05 described sessions posting "via their role token" directly to DuckBrain. Three review findings force the single-writer form instead: F-018 explicitly prefers the agent→service→DuckBrain path; F-019 rules out DuckBrain's default timestamp/UUID ordering as a durable room order; UQ-7 / OQ-14 leave sequence allocation unresolved unless the service allocates. VOL-C therefore makes the normative choice:
- **VOLC-005** Hierarchy agents **never write `/chd/*` keys directly to DuckBrain**. All room, report, audit, and work-log writes go through the invocation service's tools. The service allocates the per-room monotonic `seq`, stamps the time basis (§6.3), and writes with **its own** credential. Agent tokens authenticate **to the service**, not to DuckBrain. (This supersedes the direct-write reading of CT-05; the DuckBrain token backstop of DESIGN §6.2 layer 2 becomes defense-in-depth, not the primary enforcement.) - **VOLC-006** Because the service is the single writer, room ordering is durable by construction: `seq` values are allocated once, at write time, in commit order, and never reused (F-019 durable-sequence requirement). Allocation uses VOL-B §5.1's durable write-ahead mechanism (VOLB-028): the service reserves fsync-acked SeqHead blocks at `/chd/room/<room-id>/_head` before consuming sequence numbers — room order is the allocated-`seq` order, NEVER DuckBrain's default timestamp/UUID ordering (D4/D5 of VOL-B §1). Recovery after crash/restart re-derives "next seq" per VOLB-028 (`max(max observed message seq, last durable _head.next − 1) + 1`); an in-flight allocation that crashed before commit leaves a gap, and gaps are legal (see VOLC-018).

### 2.3 Ticket tool surface (R31-017/R31-018)
Ticket tools are controller-routed MCP operations with identical API and CLI semantics. They expose one general-purpose ticket contract for coding, research, finance, operations, incident and decision work; they do not expose a second state machine. `machine_ref` is validated against `build-spec/state-machines.json`, and `state` is the controller's projection of the canonical objective or assignment machine.
| Tool | Required input | Stored effect | Success / refusal | |---|---|---|---| | `chd_ticket_create` | `request_id`, title, kind, workflow binding, owner, criteria, graph/link refs | Atomic TicketRecord at `/chd/ticket/<id>` with `revision=1`, audit and source refs | `201`; duplicate request replays; invalid owner/graph/auth is refused before write | | `chd_ticket_get` | ticket id and read grant | Reads effective TicketRecord, last event, allowed canonical edges and consistency flags | `200`; unknown/unreadable is `404 not_found` | | `chd_ticket_update` | ticket id, `request_id`, `expected_revision`, metadata/graph/owner/criteria/link patch | CAS TicketRecord update plus audit; no implicit state transition | `200`; stale revision `409 ticket_revision_conflict`; no partial write | | `chd_ticket_transition` | ticket id, request id, expected revision, target state, reason/evidence | Atomic state projection, revision increment, immutable transition event and audit | `200`; illegal edge/writer `403 ticket_transition_not_allowed` | | `chd_ticket_query` | keyset filters and read grant | Reads ticket prefix and linked consistency state | `200` with cursor; no offset-based duplicate/missing window | | `chd_ticket_import` / `chd_ticket_export` | board rows/source digest or filters/format | Import reconciles by ticket id; export produces read-only board view | conflicts are reported; absence never deletes; export never grants authority |
Every mutation is authorized by credential principal, ticket-family scope, workflow writer and required facts before the controller writes. Every accepted mutation carries `request_id` and `correlation_id`; reports, worker runs and artifacts carry `ticket_id` plus their own `send_id`/`attempt_id`/`run_id` where relevant. A stale or mismatched correlation is a typed refusal, not a best-effort attachment. See ENDPOINTS §4.9, DATA-MODEL §1.9/§2, and VOL-E §3.
- **VOLC-007** The tool set above is the complete communication/work-log **and work-control** surface exposed to agents. Agents have **no other** path to rooms, the work log, tickets, worker runs, or the scheduler: no direct DuckBrain token in-session for `chd` writes (VOLC-005), no scheduler API access, no gateway credentials (VOLC-004). The operation inventory (every action, field, error and evidence query) is `contracts/OPERATIONS.md` (R31-025). - **VOLC-008** Tool results are structured: success returns `{ok: true, room, seq, key, thread?, wakes?}`; failure returns `{ok: false, error: {code, message, detail}}` using the error codes of §3.6 — an agent can always tell whether its write landed and where.

## 3. Four-door ingress and message contracts (F-008)

### 3.1 One surface, four doors (CT-14, RL-16)
The four doors — **API** (`POST /v1/...` HTTP), **MCP** (the MCP tool wrappers of ENDPOINTS §3.2 plus the agent tools of §2.2), **CLI** (`chd` verbs of ENDPOINTS §3.3), **webhook** (external systems via `POST /v1/signals`) — are one contract surface:
- **VOLC-009** Every operation has identical validation, authorization, idempotency, and audit semantics regardless of door. Door identity is recorded in the audit record (`door` field) and nowhere else. No door is privileged; authority comes from the credential, never the door (R-029).

### 3.2 `post` — post a message
Request payload (agent tool `chd_post`, doors API/MCP/CLI; webhook maps to `POST /v1/signals`):
```json { "from": "mgr-infra", // must equal authenticated identity (VOLC-001) "room": "obj-fleet", // existing room; membership required "to": "mgr-fleet-ops", // agent id | "group" | "@agent-id" | "owner" "kind": "msg", // msg | question | status | directive | task | report | incident "body": "non-empty human-readable text", "reply_to": null, // use chd_reply instead; null at root level "cause": { // optional causation (§5.5) "send_id": "s-20261108-1010-b3c4", "objective_id": "obj-fleet", "signal_id": "sig-..." }, "dedupe_key": "optional client key" } ```
Validation order (each failure stops with the named error):
1. Authentication → `401 unauthenticated`. 2. Identity consistency → `403 identity_mismatch` (VOLC-001). 3. Room exists **and** is readable by the caller → one `404 not_found` otherwise (VOLC-040/056). Existence and membership are deliberately indistinguishable: the check is a single lookup over the caller's authorized room set, so no response shape or timing class discloses whether a guessed id exists. The detailed denial cause is written to the audit record only (VOLC-064). 4. `kind` legality per room kind and role (§3.6 table) → `403 kind_not_allowed`. 5. `to` target exists and is a member, or is `group`/`owner` → `404 not_found`. 6. `body` non-empty, size ≤ `ingress.max_body_bytes` (default 65536) → `400 bad_request`. 7. Idempotency check → replay behavior per VOLC-017. 8. Human-approval policy for the caller (§8.4) → may hold the write in `pending_approval` (returns `202` with `approval_id`).
Success `201`:
```json { "ok": true, "room": "obj-fleet", "seq": 43, "key": "/chd/room/obj-fleet/m000000000043", "to_snapshot": ["mgr-fleet-ops"], "wakes": ["mgr-fleet-ops"], "wake_mode": "queued|dispatched" } ```

### 3.3 `reply` — reply into a thread
Same payload as `post` plus a **required** `reply_to: <seq>` identifying the parent message in the same room. The new message's `thread` resolves to the ROOT of that parent's thread (a reply to a reply carries the same root `thread` value — the tree is walked via `reply_to`, DATA-MODEL CT-12). Replying to a `kind=report` message is legal (a question about a report); replying to a message that does not exist in that room is `404 not_found`.
- **VOLC-010** The `reply_to` model is retained unchanged (RL-12/CT-12): every reply carries `reply_to` (parent seq); the root request is the thread root; nesting is unbounded; agents working one task share one subthread. There is no second threading mechanism.

### 3.4 `report` — the turn's report
Payload is the **canonical report schema v3, VOL-D §3.1**: one common envelope plus exactly one requester-selected `content` class (`free_form`, `structured`, or `dataset`). The assignment supplies `required_content`, `schema_ref` when needed, `validation_policy`, and `completion_policy`; the service copies these immutable terms into the envelope and validates before persistence. The full machine contract and positive examples are `contracts/schemas/report-v3.schema.json` and `contracts/schemas/report-v3.fixture.json`.
```json {"schema_version":3,"envelope":{"send_id":"s-20261109-1002-a1b4","attempt_id":"at-20261109-1002-c3d6","request_ref":"/chd/room/task-crier-42/m000000000043","content_digest":"sha256:...","ingest_ts":"service-stamped"},"content":{"class":"dataset","dataset_id":"ds-20261109-1102-ds01","columns":[{"name":"name","type":"string","nullable":false},{"name":"count","type":"integer","nullable":false}],"rows":[{"row_id":"r00000001","values":{"name":"alpha","count":2}},{"row_id":"r00000002","values":{"name":"beta","count":3}}],"query_contract":{"filter":"count >= 2","order_by":"row_id ASC","page_size":2,"cursor_field":"row_id"}}} ```
The waiting-for-human extension shows here (VOL-D VOLD-023 field names are canonical):
```json { "send_id": "s-20261108-1010-b3c4", "room": "task-crier-42", "status": "done | deferred | blocked | failed | waiting_human", "summary": "one paragraph, human-readable", "artifacts": ["..."], // >=1 iff status=done "reason": "...", // required iff deferred|blocked "waiting_for_human": { // required iff waiting_human "question": "approval of deploy plan", "gate_ref": "gate-deploy-1", "asked_at": "service-stamped", "requested_by": "owner" }, "next": "optional", "ts": "written by the service; agent-supplied ts ignored (VOLC-012)" } ```
- **VOLC-011** `report` is the exactly-one report per `(send_id, attempt_id)` after applying the V3 precedence in VOL-D §3.3: an exact replay is a dedupe response; a different second report while open is refused `409 report_already_posted`; a report after terminal closure is recorded as `duplicate_ignored`. Work messages (`chd_post`) in the same turn are separate writes and are unaffected (this reconciles one-write-per-room-per-turn with separate messages/reports — see §5.7). The service records the audit event for every non-replay rejection. - **VOLC-012 (v3 time/correlation).** The service stamps `seq`, `content_ref`, and `ingest_ts` from its trusted clock. Freshness is `ingest_ts >= dispatch_ts` for the same `(send_id, attempt_id, session_ref)`; agent timestamps and attached-content timestamps are evidence only. The old `report.ts >= dispatch_ts` wording is superseded by VOL-D VOLD-025. - **VOLC-013** Report validation is the verify loop's input (CT-06, ENDPOINTS §4.6): schema-fail → `422 schema_validation` (or `422 dataset_row_invalid`) and the report/dataset is NOT readable or persisted as a published report; the failed validation is audited. Unknown schema version is `422 schema_unsupported`; schema-pass is persisted and the verdict is computed by VOL-D's ladder. Exact replay, changed second report, and closed-work duplicate use VOL-D §3.3's single precedence table.

### 3.5 `read` — room log and authorized work log
`chd_read_room(room, since?, thread?, limit?)` and `chd_read_worklog(scope)` map to `GET /v1/rooms/{room}/messages` (ENDPOINTS §4.7) with cursor pagination (`since`, `limit` 1–500, response `next_since`). The **authorized work log** is defined in §5.8.
- **VOLC-014** Reads are served by the service (which enforces §8's matrix); agents do not need DuckBrain read tokens for `chd` keys. The UI chat and CLI read through the same endpoints (one read path, one enforcement point).

### 3.6 Message kinds, legality, and errors
The **complete** kind enum is seven values: `msg | question | status | directive | task | report | incident`. There is no other kind; storage (VOL-B §3.1), the §3.2 payload, tools, examples, DATA-MODEL §1.4 and this table use the same seven names.
| `kind` | Meaning | Who may post | Legal room kinds | Why | |---|---|---|---|---| | `msg` | ordinary work message | any member | objective, task, space | conversation | | `question` | a question that owes an answer in-thread; participates in missing-reply detection (§6.6) | any member | objective, task, space | explicit ask | | `status` | progress/state post, incl. waiting-for-human notices and bond-loss notices | any member; `incident`-class system notices are service-written | objective, task, space | visibility without a wake obligation | | `directive` | opens an objective; also a VP direction change inside an objective | director (opening post); VP (`message.inject`) | objective only | objective framing | | `task` | opens a task room or a task subthread | manager (in its own task/space rooms); supervisor only for a subthread inside its own task room | task, space | work assignment | | `report` | the turn's exactly-one report (`chd_report`) | any member of the room it reports into | objective, task, space | owed result | | `incident` | escalation record (R-017) | service only | objective, task, space | audit-grade escalation |
**VOLC-066 (single kind authority, R31-003).** This table is the only legality authority. Every prohibited use is refused `403 kind_not_allowed` naming `{kind, room_kind, role}`; every kind round-trips validate → store → read with the same name (round-trip test: VOLB-014 key/content match plus a read that returns the identical `kind`). Prohibited uses include: `directive` in a task or space room; `task` in an objective room; `report` from a non-member; `incident` from any agent; any kind from a principal that is not a member of the room.

### 3.7 The message state machine
Every accepted message travels one machine; each state is a durable transition recorded with the message's audit record. (Terminology note, integration pass: this is the **message state machine** — distinct from the SEND state machine of §6.4 and from the **verify ladder** rung model of VOL-D §2.4. "Ladder" alone always means the verify ladder.)
``` posted → accepted → persisted → dispatched → completed ↓ ↓ (503 path) queued (cap full — wake queued, message already durable) ```
- **posted** — the request bytes arrived at a door. - **accepted** — authenticated, validated, idempotency-claimed. Idempotent from here on: a crash after `accepted` replays the original response. - **persisted** — the service wrote `/chd/room/<room>/m<seq>` with its own credential; `seq` allocated. The caller's success response is returned at/after this state (the message survives even if the wake is lost). - **dispatched** — the router computed wake targets (§5.2) and the send orchestrator composed wake sends (which then follow the SEND state machine of §6.5). Under cap pressure the wake is `queued`, not lost — the message itself is already `persisted` (VOLC-021). - **completed** — all wakes composed; terminal for the message record. Message completion does NOT imply work completion (that is the send's verified closure, §6.5). - **VOLC-016** A crash between `accepted` and `persisted` is recovered at restart by the idempotency ledger: the request is re-executed exactly once (its dedupe record names it accepted-but-not-persisted). A crash after `persisted` never re-posts (dedupe returns the original `seq`). No accepted request is lost; no message double-posts (F-007 for the message plane; the send plane is §6.5). `persisted` means fsync-durably persisted: the write ack is the fsync'd DuckBrain append with `X-Durability == fsync` verified per the VOL-B contract (VOLB-011, VOLB-037) — a `buffered`-achieved ack on an `/chd/*` key is a hard error (F-019: the buffered default has no power-loss barrier, so an ack that does not pin and check the durability mode overpromises persistence). - **VOLC-017** Idempotency: mutating operations accept `dedupe_key`. Replay with identical body → original response, HTTP `200` (not `201`), nothing written. Replay with differing body → `409 duplicate`. Keys are scoped to the authenticated principal (mirroring Hermes' own Idempotency-Key scoping) and retained ≥ 24 h. - **VOLC-018** `seq` gaps from crashed allocations are legal and permanent; consumers must not treat gaps as lost messages. Ordering guarantee: for any two persisted messages in a room, the one with the lower `seq` committed first.

### 3.8 Artifact references and access across managers
Artifacts are references, never copies: a commit sha, a board row id, a DuckBrain work-artifact key, a file path under an agent's workspace.
- **VOLC-020** An artifact is addressable from any room, but **readable** only via the access rule: a principal may access an artifact if (a) the artifact's **home room** (the room of the message that first attached it) is one of the principal's memberships, or (b) the artifact was carried into one of the principal's rooms by an authorized cross-room reference (below). Resolution and serving happen at the service; guessed artifact ids fail `404`. - **VOLC-020a** Cross-room reference (authorized delivery handoff): an agent may attach into room B an artifact whose home is room A only if it is a member of both A and B. The service records the reference (`room_B` message `attach` pointing at the home key); recipients of B gain access to that artifact **only** — never to the rest of room A. This is how a director hands manager 1's evidence to manager 2 without opening manager 1's room. - **VOLC-020b** The director does NOT need communication tools of a subordinate to complete a delivery handoff (F-008): the reference mechanism plus a delegated sender (a communications-path agent with the configured delivery capability, D-011) is the contract. Delegation of *sending* is a grant (§8.3), not a tool copy.

## 4. Session mapping — provisioning, and which event chooses NEW vs REUSE (F-010, D-025)
Work-thread identity (room + `reply_to` tree in DuckBrain) and Hermes session identity (`session_key`/`X-Hermes-Session-Id`) are distinct (D-014).

### 4.1 Provisioning is not delivery (R31-022)
Two independent decisions are made for every wake:
- **Provisioning** — how a session that does not yet exist comes into being: `fresh` (continuation-less create) or `fork` (created from a parent session at a recorded `fork_point_seq`, VOL-B §7.5). Fork is used when a task subthread must inherit the assigner's working context; it is a native Hermes session operation, never a delivery mode. - **Delivery** — how an already-provisioned session receives this wake: `NEW` (the session's first turn) or `REUSE` (a continuation turn).
A forked session still receives its assignment as `NEW` (first turn). There is no third delivery mode, and `fork ≠ delivery` survives into every table, figure and API. Each bond (VOL-B §3.3) records which provisioning produced it (`fork_mode`, `parent_bond_id`) and each send manifest records the delivery `mode`.

## 5. Reply, group, and fan-out semantics (F-009)

### 5.1 Recipient snapshot policy
- **VOLC-025** At post time the service expands `to` into an immutable `to_snapshot` stored on the message: `to: "<agent-id>"` → `[id]`; `to: "@id"` → `[id]`; `to: "group"` → all current members **minus the sender**; `to: "owner"` → the VP principal(s) configured for that room. Later membership changes never alter a past message's snapshot (audit stability). Notification/wake decisions use the snapshot; read access always follows current membership (§8.2).

### 5.2 Notification and wake rules
- **VOLC-026** Targeting decides **who is WOKEN**, never who can read (RL-6). The router wakes exactly the snapshot targets, each wake composing a send that obeys per-gateway `max_inflight` and per-agent `max_sessions` (CT-13): at capacity the wake queues (`429 at_capacity` on the interactive path; message stays `persisted`). The sender's own wake is suppressed (no self-echo, RL-6) — including the owner. - **VOLC-027** `kind=question` messages participate in missing-reply detection like any send: the addressed target must reply in-thread or report by `verify.deadline_s`, else CT-11's mechanical detection fires (notify caller + bump, riding §5.1's ladder, counted `missing_reply_total`).

### 5.3 Group expansion and one accountable owner
- **VOLC-028** A directive sent to a **group** of managers expands into one send per recipient (each with its own `send_id`, its own ladder, its own report). Each send names exactly one **accountable owner** (the recipient agent). A deliverable therefore has either one owner, or N sends each with its own owner — never a group-owned deliverable. The parent's aggregation record (§5.6) tracks the set. - **VOLC-029** Duplicates and partial replies are handled deterministically: duplicate reports for the same `send_id` are refused (VOLC-011); a recipient that closes `verified` while siblings are still open leaves the aggregation open; a sibling that fails or escalates follows its own ladder without re-waking the closed sibling. The aggregation completes only when every child send is in a terminal state (§5.6).

### 5.4 Causation and correlation ids
Tickets are the stable join key for both coding and non-coding work. Every service-created ticket operation also carries `request_id` and `correlation_id`; worker/report operations carry `ticket_id` alongside `objective_id`, `assignment_id`, `send_id`, `attempt_id`, `run_id`, `session_ref`, and `artifact_ref` where applicable. The controller persists these values in the TicketRecord `meta` object, audit event, and linked CHD record. A report or artifact with a mismatched ticket or send is rejected as `bad_report` or `ticket_link_conflict`, never heuristically attached. Correlation ids are opaque, stable across retries, and do not authorize access.
- **VOLC-030** Every service-created entity carries correlation ids: `objective_id` (root), `send_id` (per wake), `signal_id` (ingress), `report_id`, `run_id` (Hermes run, when known). Messages may carry `cause {send_id?, objective_id?, signal_id?}` (§3.2). A report echoes the `send_id` it answers; its `content_ref` pins the message key. Correlation ids are immutable and are the join keys for every audit and aggregation query (F-009 causation/correlation requirement).

### 5.5 Cross-room upward references
- **VOLC-031** An upward report (supervisor→manager, manager→director) may carry `up_ref: {room, seq}` referencing the subthread that justifies it. Upward means **child-room → parent-room along the hierarchy that created the rooms**; the service validates that the referencing agent is a member of both rooms and that the parent relation holds (objective→task lineage is recorded at room creation). Recipients gain read access to the referenced thread only (same reference-grant semantics as VOLC-020a). Downward and lateral references without dual membership are refused `404 not_found` — the referenced room is treated as nonexistent for that caller (the same single non-member contract as §3.2, R31-002); the detailed denial cause is recorded in the audit record only.

### 5.6 Completion aggregation
- **VOLC-032** For a fan-out (group directive or multi-child objective), the service maintains an aggregation record on the parent send: children, per-child state, and an aggregate state = `open | all_verified | partially_closed{detail} | any_escalated`. Each child entry names the child `send_id` and the child thread it resolves to `(room, subthread_root)` — and **each supervisor result resolves to exactly one child thread**: the child `send_id` maps to one bond (VOL-B §3.3) whose identity tuple fixes one `(room, subthread_root)`; a send that resolves to zero or multiple threads is refused `409 thread_not_owned` (VOLB-063) and can never enter the aggregation. The parent's own report/acceptance flow (VOL-D) consumes only the aggregate state; the director never polls child rooms to learn it. A drained subtree (every child `deferred{reason: drained}`) aggregates to `deferred{drained}` per DESIGN §5.6. The worked end-to-end trace with exact record ids is fixture VOLB-072 (VOL-B §7.5).

### 5.7 One write per room per turn, reconciled
- **VOLC-033** The handbook's one-write-per-room-per-turn rule is normative **for reports**: exactly one `report` per (send, turn) per room (VOLC-011). Work messages (`msg`, `question`) are separate, individually-sequence writes and may be many per turn; the report, when the turn owes one, is the agent's **last** write to that room in that turn (the service enforces ordering by rejecting a work message posted after the turn's report: `409 report_already_posted` guards the tail).

### 5.8 Authorized work-log discovery
- **VOLC-034** "The overall work log" an invocation can discover = **authorized context only**: (a) every room the agent is a member of, (b) every subthread in those rooms, (c) every artifact/thread explicitly referenced into those rooms (VOLC-020a/VOLC-031). It is **never** "all rooms" (D-014 scope note; F-009 completion evidence: global ≠ unrelated-room access). `chd_read_worklog` returns rooms (a) and merged references (c) with per-room cursors; the service computes the set from current membership + recorded references — an agent cannot widen it, and a guessed room id simply is not in the set (it gets `404`, not a leak). - **VOLC-035** The work log persists across invocations: because it is derived from durable membership and reference records (not from session memory), a NEW session (W1/W2/W8/W10) re-discovers the same authorized log. This is the mechanism that makes fresh sessions usable without history reconstruction.

## 6. Scheduler admission and send state machines (F-011)

### 6.1 Clock registration and time basis
**Plain-prose operation.** The service triggers registration at startup or config change. It reads the validated trigger configuration and scheduler clock, checks lane identity and clock skew, writes the registration result and effective timestamps, and uses those timestamps for deadlines. Normal example: `chd-mgr-m1` is registered and its callback carries the scheduler timestamp. Failure example: clock skew exceeds the configured bound; the readiness check writes an alarm and refuses silent deadline processing.
- **VOLC-036** All timed work is registered as NORMAL scheduler trigger lanes (CT-02/RL-1) at service startup and on config change, landed through the scheduler's validated config path (R-014). Lane identities are stable: `chd-<cycle>` for the director sync, `chd-mgr-<agent-id>` for per-manager clocks, `chd-followup-<send-id>` for follow-up timers (§6.6). The service owns **no clock of its own** and never runs a local scheduler. - **VOLC-037** Time basis: the **scheduler's clock** is authoritative. All service-recorded timestamps (`dispatch_ts`, deadlines, `ts`) are RFC 3339 UTC taken from the service host, which MUST be NTP-synced against the same source as the scheduler; deadline comparisons use the timestamps the service itself stamped (never agent clocks). Drift beyond `ingress.max_clock_skew_s` (default 5 s) is a startup readiness failure (alarm, not silent tolerance). The accepted cycle boundary is the scheduler fire callback: `cycle_start=ts` on the `/v1/cycle` record and `cycle_end` is recorded only after all sends composed by that fire reach a terminal or waiting state. Startup-to-first-status is outside the cycle and is measured separately; a cycle cannot be inferred from a process restart, endpoint wake, or counter snapshot.
- **Clock-boundary readback.** Registration evidence names `lane_id`, `schedule`, `clock_source: scheduler`, `registered_at`, `config_digest` and `last_fire_ts`; an acceptance query must read the scheduler registration and the cycle ledger together. The service owns no local clock or hidden cycle boundary.

### 6.2 Timed callback contract (`POST /v1/cycle`)
**Plain-prose operation.** The scheduler triggers the callback with its lane, cycle, timestamp, and dedupe key. The service reads the callback ledger and pending work, checks the credential and dedupe key, writes composed sends and deadlines with fsync, and returns 2xx only after the durable acknowledgement. Normal example: a replayed fire returns the retained response without composing a second send. Failure example: persistence fails; the service returns 5xx, writes no false success, and lets the scheduler retry the same dedupe key.
The scheduler's fire is the callback of CT-02 (schema per ENDPOINTS §3.4): `{cycle, lane, namespace, ts, dedupe_key}`.
- **VOLC-038** Auth: the scheduler callback credential only; failure is `401`, terminal, no retry flood (FACT-12). A replayed `dedupe_key` (same lane, same fire) returns the recorded original response — the cycle is **not** re-executed (idempotent fire). - **VOLC-039** Ack point and 2xx semantics: the service returns `2xx` to the scheduler when the fire has been **durably acknowledged** — the cycle's work items (sends to compose, deadlines to arm) are persisted fsync-durably with `X-Durability == fsync` verified (VOL-B VOLB-011/ VOLB-037; the buffered default has no power-loss barrier — F-019), so a crash after the 2xx loses nothing. The 2xx body reports `sends_composed` / `sends_queued` / `bump_requests` truthfully; "all queued under backpressure" is still a valid `2xx` (the callback itself succeeded; ENDPOINTS §3.4). `5xx` is returned only when the service could not persist the ack — in that case the scheduler's retry re-fires and dedupe makes it safe. - **VOLC-040** Retry: the scheduler retries transport/5xx failures with its own bounded backoff; the service applies no additional retry to callbacks (one mechanism only). A callback that exhausts the scheduler's retries is visible as a gap in the cycle ledger and counted `cycle_fire_failures_total` — it never silently skips deadline arithmetic: deadlines are absolute (VOLC-037), so a late fire still evaluates correctly.

### 6.3 Bump/admission results, fairness, queue persistence
**Plain-prose operation.** The harness or authorized immediate requester triggers admission through the scheduler bump or the bounded run-now path. It reads manifests, caps, gateway capacity, and the shared reservation ledger; checks permissions and dedupe identity; writes `admitted`, `queued`, `expired`, or named refusal; and exposes the result to the caller. Normal example: full capacity produces a durable queued manifest that the next fair cycle dispatches. Failure example: a duplicate request uses the same assignment identity; the ledger returns the retained reservation and the harness sends no second gateway request.
- **VOLC-041** Admission for a wake is requested ONLY via the scheduler bump API (`POST /api/v1/projects/{name}/bump`, FACT-14) or the owner-approved `wake_once` extension (Q-6) — R-003/R-018. The service records per send an admission result: `admitted | queued | expired | refused{reason}`. `refused` occurs only on contract errors (unknown lane, auth gate) and is an incident; capacity never refuses — capacity queues (RL-15). - **VOLC-042** Fairness: within one gateway queue, sends dispatch FIFO by `composed_ts` with aging (a queued send's effective priority rises with wait time so a steady stream of new sends cannot starve an old one); across gateways, dispatch is independent (fan-out, §3.4). `orchestration.max_fanout` bounds wakes composed per cycle (default 12). - **VOLC-043** Queue persistence: the send queue IS the DuckBrain send manifests (`/chd/send/<send-id>/manifest`, state `queued`). A restart re-derives the queue from manifests; nothing queues only in memory. Crash windows: manifest written before admission request → a crash between the two re-derives as "admission request not yet sent" (re-request; bump idempotent per `dedupe_key`); no admitted-but-unrecorded state can exist, so no admission capacity can leak (F-007 evidence for the send plane).

### 6.4 The SEND state machine (complete)
**Plain-prose operation.** The send orchestrator triggers each transition from a durable manifest. It reads the current state and transition evidence, checks the guard and owner, writes the next state before the external effect, and emits the matching metric and audit record. Normal example: a fresh correlated report changes `await_report` to `verified` and closes the send. Failure example: a transport check fails before delivery; the orchestrator writes `paused:unreachable`, holds the deadline and capacity, and resumes only after a healthy check.
Owner of every transition: the **send orchestrator** (service). Each send row is the manifest; all states are durable before effects.
``` ┌──────────┐ admission ┌──────────┐ gateway 2xx ┌────────────┐ composed ──▶ queued ├─────────────▶─ admitted ├────────────▶─ dispatched │ (per wake) └──────────┘ accepted └──────────┘ └─────┬──────┘ │ │ 2×cycle expiry │ gateway terminal error │ verify.deadline_s │ ▼ ▼ ▼ │ deferred{backpressure} failed{dispatch_error} ┌─────────────┐ │ ▲ ▲ │ await_report │ │ │ │ └─┬────┬──────┘ │ re-queued by next cycle │ fresh report │ │ no report / bad report │ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ │ ┌──────────┐ verify ladder (VOL-D §2.4) │ │ │ │ verified │──▶ closed{verified} │ │ │ └──────────┘ │ │ │ │ escalate rung 2 ──▶ closed{escalated} │ │ │ │ │ │ valid waiting_human report │ │ ▼ │ │ ┌─────────┐ resolution evidence │ │ │ waiting │──────────────▶ composed (successor) ▼ │ └─────────┘ cancelled ◀───────┴──────────────────────────┘ (any pre-dispatch state, VP/director only) ```
- **VOLC-044** States and owners (every state names entry, exit, recovery; F-011 completion evidence). The bullets are **generated** from `build-spec/state-machines.json` (the machine canon, schema `state-machines.schema.json`) by `tools/gen_state_machines.py`; `tools/check_state_machines.py` proves the chart above and these bullets equal the canon: <!-- SM-CANON:SEND-STATES:BEGIN --> - `composed` — wake decided, manifest written. Exit: queued or cancelled. Recovery: none needed (not yet effective). - `queued` — durable in manifest, awaiting admission. Exit: `admitted`, `deferred{backpressure}` (2×cycle expiry), or `cancelled`. Recovery: re-derived from manifest at restart (VOLC-043). - `admitted` — bump accepted. Exit: `dispatched` (gateway 2xx) or `failed{dispatch_error}` (terminal auth rejection, FACT-12) or back to `queued` (scheduler admitted the lane but did not pick the send before expiry). - `dispatched` — gateway accepted the POST. Exit: `await_report`. Recovery: scheduler's orphan-scan/CONTINUATION machinery (FACT-29); a send still `dispatched` past `verify.deadline_s` enters the ladder as `no_report`. - `await_report` — report expected by `dispatch_ts + verify.deadline_s`. Exit: `verified`, `waiting`, or ladder entry (`no_report`/`bad_report`). - `waiting` — a valid `waiting_human` report closed the current attempt and opened a durable wait. The logical send remains non-terminal. Exit: `composed` only after recorded resolution evidence mints a successor attempt; timers never resume it. - `verified` — a FRESH valid report closed the send (`report.ts >= dispatch_ts`, machine-checked, R-031). A deferred send is dropped from the active queue; the next scheduled cycle supersedes it (no unbounded queue). Not a failure; counted `sends_deferred{reason}`. - `failed` — `failed{reason}` — terminal failure: `dispatch_error`, `report_failed` (explicit `status: failed` report), ladder exhausted → escalates before closing. Every failure names its reason and is counted. - `cancelled` — VP or (within delegated authority) director cancels a send in any pre-`await_report` state; the manifest records who and why. Cancellation of an in-flight wake is best-effort: the manifest is closed `cancelled` and, if the gateway call had not been made, nothing dispatches; if it had, the ladder is stopped and the agent's eventual report is accepted but marked `cancelled` (work may have run — cancellation is not retroactive erasure; audit keeps the lineage). - `closed` — `closed{reason}` — terminal: `verified | escalated | expired`. Every closure writes a durable record (R-017 analog). <!-- SM-CANON:SEND-STATES:END --> - **VOLC-045** Queue expiry and "cycle": the 2×cycle staleness of DESIGN §3.4 is defined as **2 × the cooldown interval of the trigger lane that owns the send's cycle** — for the director sync cycle, twice the director lane's cron period; for a message-driven send with no owning lane, `orchestration.stale_after_s` (default floor 60 s, set to the hierarchy's nominal cycle). The owning lane id is stored on the manifest at compose time, so expiry is computable even if config changes later. A paused send's deadline arithmetic is suspended (deadline = dispatch + deadline_s measured over non-paused time), so an outage does not convert into `no_report` failures.

### 6.5 Waiting-for-human vs failures (D-012)
**Plain-prose operation.** The harness triggers this path when a report declares `waiting_human` or when the deadline finds silence. It reads the report status, gate id, attempt, and current manifest; checks whether the report is valid and whether approval evidence exists; writes the wait record and terminal attempt; and propagates the wait upstream. Normal example: a valid gate question closes the current attempt, opens `/chd/wait/<gate-id>`, and later mints a successor attempt after recorded approval. Failure example: a timer expires without approval; the harness escalates visibility, writes no approval, does not resume, and never counts the wait as `missing_reply`.
- **VOLC-047** *(superseded by VOLC-067 — kept for lineage; do not implement the `closed{waiting}`-for-the-send reading).* - **VOLC-067 (wait closes the ATTEMPT, not the send — R31-005).** `status: waiting_human` is a valid report outcome, not a failure. On a valid waiting report the harness: 1. closes the **current attempt** as `closed{waiting}` (attempt-level terminal; its `attempt_id` never reopens); 2. releases the attempt's capacity slot, because the attempt is provably finished (a report arrived; nothing is still executing); 3. creates the durable wait record `/chd/wait/<gate-id>` = `{gate_id, send_id, attempt_id, agent, question, requested_by, asked_at, state: waiting|resolved|cancelled, resolved_at?, resolution_ref?}`; 4. records the logical send in the machine's `waiting` state (the send is non-terminal), so ownership and obligation survive; the state-machine successor edge is `waiting → composed`, never `await_report → composed`; 5. retains `send_id`, `gate_id`, `attempt_id`, the target snapshot, report correlation, and wait record indefinitely until resolution/cancellation; 6. propagates the wait upward as `kind=status` notices carrying the same `gate_id` (supervisor → manager → director), and sets the objective's aggregate waiting marker.
**Wait semantics table (normative):**
| Item | Waiting attempt | Logical send / successor | |---|---|---| | Terminality | Current `attempt_id` is terminal and never reopens | Send remains open in machine state `waiting` | | Capacity | Slot released only because a correlated report proves this attempt stopped | No slot is reserved while the wait is unresolved | | Correlation | Retain `send_id`, `attempt_id`, `gate_id`, target snapshot, report ref, and wait record | Successor links `supersedes_attempt_id` and keeps the same `send_id` | | Resume mode | No automatic resume; timer/follow-up is visibility only | Recorded resolution mints a NEW attempt/session-target and composes `queued` | | Post-resume evidence | None can be inferred from approval | Fresh successor report, correlation, artifact, and criteria checks are required for `verified` | | Approval | Required guard evidence for the resume edge | Approval alone is never a verified work result |
The wait table is normative: the current attempt is terminal, the logical send remains open, the slot is released only because the report proves this attempt stopped, and resume requires a NEW successor attempt plus a fresh correlated report. Approval evidence is necessary to resume but is never itself a verified work result; the successor's report still requires normal criteria/artifact checks.
On recorded resolution (explicit approval, or a prior authorization the director holds for that specific gate, recorded with its authority ref), the harness mints a **successor attempt** — new `attempt_id`, `attempt+1`, same `send_id` — composes it as NEW (W12), and the resumed work must post a fresh report for the successor attempt. Approval alone never yields `verified`: only the successor attempt's fresh, correlated report can close the send. A wait timeout changes nothing: it is visibility escalation (VOL-D §3.4), never approval, never a close, never an auto-resume. - **VOLC-048** Silence is never approval: no timer, timeout, or expiry grants an approval gate (D-012; Q-006: the per-assignment completion/approval condition governs, and an explicit stop-until-approval gate must hold). A waiting_human chain advances only on (a) explicit human action through a VP surface, or (b) prior authorization the director holds for that specific gate (then the director continues and records which authorization it used). The **approval gate itself has no expiry** — waiting resolution always requires recorded approval evidence. The wait-level timers are visibility mechanisms only and never resolve anything: VOL-C's single bounded follow-up (§6.6) asks the waiting agent; VOL-D's `verify.wait_timeout_s` (VOLD-023) re-enters the **verify ladder at rung 2** when a wait stays unresolved — an escalation for visibility (incident to parent room / owner page), never an approval, never a close, never an auto-resume. VOLC-067's closed waiting attempt and the wait record persist until human resolution regardless of any timer. - **VOLC-049** Counted failures vs valid waits: waiting_human reports are excluded from `missing_reply_total`, ladder rung counts, and dry-run-throttle artifact counting; they increment `waits_opened_total`/`waits_resolved_total`. A send that produces neither report nor waiting_human by deadline is `no_report` (a failure path) — the distinction is mechanical on the report's `status` field.

### 6.6 Follow-up timers without reminder loops (D-012, RL-11 interplay)
**Plain-prose operation.** The service triggers at most one follow-up lane for a wait record. It reads the gate state and follow-up count, checks that the wait changed and the cap is not exceeded, writes one question and its audit record, and leaves the wait unresolved. Normal example: one question asks whether the agent still needs the gate and the count increments once. Failure example: the gate is unchanged after the question; the service writes no second timer, does not reset the wait, and does not page repeatedly.
- **VOLC-050** A wait record may arm **at most one** follow-up timer per gate per waiting agent, registered as a `chd-followup-<gate-id>` trigger lane at a configured interval (`verify.followup_after_s`, default 86400). When it fires, the service sends ONE follow-up message (a `question` kind: "still waiting on <gate>?") to the waiting agent's room — and that is all: the fire does not reset the wait, does not increment ladder counters, and does not re-page anyone. - **VOLC-051** Loop bound: a waiting agent may answer a follow-up with a fresh waiting_human report **only if** the wait record changed (new gate id or an explicit human contact recorded); an unchanged wait does NOT re-arm a new timer (the gate has one live follow-up timer, ever). Total follow-ups per gate are capped at `verify.max_followups` (default 2); beyond the cap the service stops and the wait simply persists until human resolution. There is no path by which follow-up timers compose into repeated wake cycles (no uncontrolled reminder loops). - **VOLC-052** Missing-reply vs waiting: CT-11's mechanical detection treats a `waiting_human` report (or a `question` reply) as "the reply came"; only true silence after `verify.deadline_s` starts the notify-caller + bump ladder. A target that answered with waiting_human is reported to the caller as `waiting`, never as `missing`.

### 6.7 Dual admission: enqueue-only and run-now (R31-019, D-022, D-029)
The scheduler is **not** the only initiator. A supervisor (or a director on a delegated path) may do exactly two things with a foreman assignment:
| Operation | Meaning | Effect on the target | |---|---|---| | `enqueue_only` | place the work in the queue; a later scheduled wake picks it up | message + manifest persisted; **no gateway call now** | | `run_now` | request execution as soon as capacity permits | same durable records, plus an immediate dispatch attempt |
**VOLC-073 (two operations, one contract).** Both operations are called on the controller (`POST /v1/assignments` with `admission: enqueue_only | run_now`, tool `chd_assign`). They share: authorization (the caller must hold `foreman.assign` or its own tier's assign right), the same assignment/ticket records, the same per-gateway and per-agent capacity, the same send/attempt identity and the same audit. `enqueue_only` never forces a wake; `run_now` never bypasses capacity.
**Capacity and admission ownership — N-1 PROPOSED (not user-confirmed).** The design choice is where an immediate request is admitted. The proposal, marked as proposed because the user expressly left it open:
- **Single admission point per gateway, owned by the controller.** The controller holds the authoritative, durable capacity ledger for each gateway and agent, derived from send manifests exactly as §3.4 does (no second counter). A `run_now` request performs one atomic compare-and-reserve: `reserve(send_id, gateway, agent) → ok | at_capacity | duplicate`. - **Scheduler cooperation, not duplication.** A timed wake still arrives through the scheduler's bump path; the controller's reservation is the same primitive for both producers, so the two paths cannot both claim the same slot. Where the deployment requires scheduler-granted admission, the controller issues the bump and records `admission_source: scheduler`; where it runs controller-local admission, it records `admission_source: controller_local`. Both are visible in the manifest, so an operator can see which path ran. - **Why this shape:** one ledger, two producers, one atomic reservation. Two independent ledgers (scheduler count + controller count) would each be correct alone and wrong together — that is the exact double-dispatch failure R31-019 requires us to prevent. - **Reversible default:** `admission.run_now_owner: "controller_local"` with `admission.scheduler_bump_fallback: true`. If the deployment's scheduler is the only holder of admission authority, flip the first value; the reservation primitive and the manifests do not change. - **Race rule:** timed tick and `run_now` for the same assignment are ordered by the reservation primitive; the loser observes `duplicate` and returns the winner's `send_id`/`attempt_id` (idempotent, never a second attempt). - **Failure behaviour:** controller cannot reach the capacity store → `503 admission_unavailable`, nothing dispatched, request stays `queued` (never silently dropped); scheduler unreachable on the bump path → backoff and retry, same dedupe key. - **Recovery:** restart re-derives the ledger from manifests; a reservation without a manifest write is invisible and therefore harmless; a manifest without a reservation is re-admitted once (dedupe by `send_id`).
**Full-cap response.** `run_now` at cap returns `202 {state: "queued", reason: "at_capacity", queue_position}` for an interactive caller and `429 at_capacity` for a synchronous one; in both cases the message and manifest are durable and the send is dispatched when a slot frees. `enqueue_only` always returns `202 {state: "queued"}`.
**Duplicate request identity.** Every request carries `request_id`; replay with the same `request_id` returns the original manifest ids and performs no new work. Two different request ids that name the same logical unit of work (same ticket + same assignee + same open send) are refused `409 duplicate` with the existing `send_id`, so a supervisor retry cannot double-dispatch an assignment.
**Race tests (acceptance).** Concurrent scheduler tick + `run_now` for one assignment under cap 1 → exactly one dispatch, one attempt, one manifest; the other producer observes `duplicate`. Same race with cap already full → both queue, one dispatch on release, no lost request.

### 6.9 Scheduler surface summary (what VOL-C adds to it)
Nothing in VOL-C changes scheduler scheduling algorithms (R-003/R-018): the scheduler still runs its lanes, cooldowns and bump API. What VOL-C adds is a controller-side reservation for the second initiator (§6.7, N-1 PROPOSED) plus the trigger lanes named per VOLC-036, the callback contract VOLC-038..040, and the bump-result bookkeeping VOLC-041..043. `wake_once` remains owner-gated (Q-6) and, if adopted, slots into VOLC-041 without changing this volume.

## 7. Managed worker dispatch and run control (R31-021, D-024)
The CLI launch prescription is replaced. A foreman no longer shells out to `hermes chat -q` from its own session; it calls one structured, HTTP-backed operation that the controller executes against the correct gateway and profile.

### 7.1 Transport decision (documented, not assumed)
**VOLC-074.** Worker dispatch SHALL be `foreman → controller → gateway`. The foreman calls the controller's dispatch endpoint with its own service token; the controller validates authority and capacity, then performs the gateway POST with its gateway credential, exactly as it does for any other wake (harness-only write rule, VOLC-005). A direct foreman→gateway transport is NOT part of this revision; if a deployment enables it, it must be an explicitly authorized, configured route (`worker.direct_gateway: true`) that still uses the controller's reservation and audit, and it is out of the rev-2.0 conformance envelope. Hermes-native delegation tools that inherit the foreman's runtime are explicitly **not** the contract: they share the foreman's profile and provider, which D-023 forbids for workers.

### 7.2 Dispatch request contract
`POST /v1/workers/dispatch` (tool `chd_worker_dispatch`), agent principal only:
```json { "request_id": "wr-20261109-1015-a1b2", "worker": { "agent_id": "wrk-crier-03", "profile": "chd-worker-crier-03", "role": "worker" }, "work": { "ticket_id": "CRIER-412", "assignment_id": "a-...", "room": "task-crier-42", "thread_root": 41, "send_id": "s-...", "parent_bond_id": "b-..." }, "instructions": { "body_ref": "/chd/room/task-crier-42/m000000000041", "criteria_ref": "CRIER-412#criteria", "inline_instructions": "optional bounded text" }, "workspace": { "workdir": "/srv/work/crier-412", "scope": ["repo", "tmp"] }, "runtime": { "provider": "deepseek", "model": "deepseek-flash", "context_window": 160000, "max_turns": 40 }, "provisioning": { "mode": "fresh | fork", "fork_point_seq": 41 }, "admission": { "mode": "run_now | enqueue_only" }, "dedupe_key": "CRIER-412:attempt:1" } ```
| Field | Type | Required | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | `request_id` | string | yes | Idempotency identity; replay returns the same run | | `worker.agent_id` / `worker.profile` | string | yes | Profile MUST be non-default and distinct; sharing is `422 profile_not_distinct` | | `work.*` | strings | yes | Must resolve to live records, and the caller must own/be authorized on them | | `instructions.body_ref` | key | yes | The assignment message; the worker reads it itself (no prompt synthesis) | | `instructions.inline_instructions` | string | no | ≤ 8 KiB, recorded verbatim | | `workspace.workdir` | abs path | yes | Must be inside the worker's configured allowed roots (`422 workspace_not_allowed`) | | `runtime.*` | strings/ints | no | Absent = worker's configured runtime; present = must be within the caller's delegation pool | | `provisioning.mode` | enum | yes | `fork` requires `fork_point_seq` and a live parent session | | `admission.mode` | enum | yes | §6.7 semantics | | `dedupe_key` | string | yes | One logical dispatch |
**VOLC-075.** The controller validates in this order: authentication → caller role (foreman or above) → work-record existence and ownership → worker profile distinctness and existence → workspace allowed root → runtime within pool → admission → dispatch. A rejection names one error from §3.6 and writes an audit row; it writes no run record.

### 7.3 Run identity, status, progress, result
**VOLC-076.** Each dispatch creates a durable `WorkerRun` record:
``` { run_id: "wrun-...", request_id, send_id, attempt_id, worker, profile, gateway, workspace, state: queued|admitted|running|succeeded|failed| cancelled|uncertain|unreachable, started_ts, ended_ts?, exit_reason?, progress: {last_beat_ts, turns, tokens, artifacts[]}, result_ref: {room, seq} | null } ```
at `/chd/worker/<run_id>`. Reads: `GET /v1/workers/runs/{run_id}` (owner foreman, director, VP). Progress is a heartbeat write at most once per `worker.progress_interval_s` (default 60); it is observation, never a completion claim. The **result** is the worker's report posted into its task room (`kind=report`, correlated `send_id`); the run becomes `succeeded` only when that report is verified (CT-06) — a process exit code is not a verdict.
**VOLC-077 (asynchrony).** Dispatch returns `202 {run_id, state}` immediately. The foreman may poll the run, read the room, or wait for the wake-on-report; it must not block its own turn on worker completion.

### 7.4 Cancel, timeout, recovery
**VOLC-078.** `POST /v1/workers/runs/{run_id}/cancel` (foreman/director, or VP) performs: mark `cancelled` intent → `POST /v1/runs/{run_id}/stop` on the gateway → await run-status confirmation (VOLB-060) → release the slot only on `proven-stopped`. Cancellation is not retroactive erasure: work already produced stays as artifacts and the report (if any) is kept, annotated `cancelled`. Timeout uses the same path when `runtime.max_turns` or `worker.timeout_s` is exceeded, with `exit_reason: timeout`.
**VOLC-079 (restart and retry).** The request/run pair is idempotent: a controller restart re-reads `queued|admitted` runs and re-drives them; `running` runs are reconciled by run status exactly as sends are (VOLB-060). Retry of a dispatch with the same `request_id` returns the original `run_id`; a retry with a new `request_id` for the same `(ticket, worker, attempt)` is refused `409 duplicate`. A failed run never silently becomes a second worker launch: the foreman decides whether to retry, and the audit shows both runs.

### 7.5 Foreman verification handoff
The foreman's own verification loop is unchanged (D-004): it reads the worker's report, samples artifacts, runs its gates, and posts exactly one final report for its own send (VOL-A-016). What changes is only the *launch* mechanism: no shell, no CLI process wrangling, no inherited environment. The worker's separate profile, provider credentials, session store and workspace come from its own configuration (D-023, VOL-D Pt II).

## 8. Enforceable authorization (F-012)

### 8.1 The three VP grants, named separately (CT-10/R-026)
VP authority is exactly three grants, configured and enforced separately:
1. **`objective.create`** — open objective rooms (VP-supplied directives). 2. **`message.inject`** — post messages (any legal kind except `incident`) into rooms the VP may touch. 3. **`room.read`** — read rooms the VP may touch.
Each is a boolean in `vp.grants` with an independent room scope list (`vp.grants.rooms` — config data, never discovered). ENDPOINTS §2's "default-allow" language is hereby scoped: a VP token enables the **operation classes** it holds, within the **configured room scope**; the owner's full-access VP token is simply one configured instance where all three grants are true with the full room list. (Reconciles ENDPOINTS §2 with DESIGN §11.1; DESIGN is normative.)
- **VOLC-053** The three grants are independent: a VP with read but not inject gets read-only; with inject but not create can post into existing rooms only. Enforcement is per operation at the service boundary, and each denied attempt is audited with the grant that was missing. - **VOLC-054** Harness-internal agents are **default-deny as VP** (R-026): an agent token presenting `as: "vp"` or calling a VP-only endpoint is refused `403 vp_identity_misuse`, audited, and counted as an integrity violation (§6.3).

### 8.3 The four authority classes, including meta-grant (D-009, D-016, D-032)
Permissions are four independently held classes; possessing one never implies another:
- **use** — may exercise the operation/tool/resource itself; - **grant_use** — may confer (parts of) a `use` permission from a named **allowed pool** onto subordinate agents within a named **scope**; - **meta_grant** — may confer **authority to delegate further** (the right to make grantors), bounded by `recipient_scope` and `downstream_rights`; - **create** — may create subordinate agents (per D-005 setting; lower-tier policy OPEN, §11.1).
- **VOLC-057** A grantor may hold `grant` on a pool containing tools it cannot `use` (D-009 is normative; Q-008 boundary: wording — skill or role text — never substitutes for the effective grant). Conversely `use` never implies `grant`, and skill wording alone is **never** an effective grant (F-012): effective permissions are computed exclusively from config grants and recorded `GrantRecord`s; skill text, prompts, and role descriptions are ignored by the enforcement layer. - **VOLC-058** Grant origins, recorded on every effective permission: `vp_configured` (VP-configured grants are already granted — no director grant needed, D-016), `director_grant` (on-demand, valid only within the director's delegatable authority) and `manager_grant` (a manager that itself holds `grant_use`/`meta_grant` within its scope). **VP configuration wins conflicts** with any delegation (D-016): enforcement computes `effective = vp_configured ∪ (derived ∩ delegatable_authority)`, and a derived grant can never widen anything a VP setting narrows. - **VOLC-059** Grant lifecycle: created via the service's grant operation (audited), scoped (capability + resource scope + optional expiry), revocable by the granting agent or immediately by any VP. **Revocation does not reach into an existing session**: enforcement for a live session uses its `SessionPolicySnapshot` (VOLB-051, §8.9); future sessions resolve current grants and therefore drop revoked-derived rights. Forked-session behavior is not inferred from the word "future": the explicit two-mode rule and existing/future classification are VOLC-069/§8.9 and VOLB-051. All grants — VP-configured and dynamic — appear in the effective readback (§8.7/§8.9) with their origin and lineage.
- **VOLC-068 (meta-grant, R31-026).** A `meta_grant` record carries `capability`, `resource_scope`, `recipient_scope` (roles/agents/tiers), `downstream_rights ⊆ {use, grant_use, meta_grant}` and `lineage`. Issuance rules: 1. the grantor must itself hold `meta_grant` for that capability and scope, and the issuance must cite it as `authority_ref`; 2. the new grant's capability, scope, recipients and downstream rights must be a **subset** of the grantor's authority — no self-expansion, no widening, no third-party substitution; 3. lineage is appended and immutable; cycles are rejected; 4. VP configuration is the root authority and can neither be exceeded nor revoked by a derived grant. Rejections: `403 meta_grant_exceeds_authority`, `403 grant_outside_pool`, `409 grant_cycle`. Issuance, rejection, replay (same `dedupe_key` → original grant id) and revocation are audited; `GET /v1/policy/effective` shows each grant's `kind`, `origin`, `authority_ref` and lineage. Delegation applies to tools, skills, room/ticket/archive storage and profile/state operations alike — one model, four classes; the resource vocabulary differs, the semantics do not.
- **VOLC-068a (delegation of grant in practice).** Four acceptance cases must behave as stated: (a) user without the grant cannot call; (b) grantor without use can grant, cannot call; (c) grantor without meta-grant cannot mint another grantor; (d) authorized delegation-of-grant succeeds only within the issuer's recipient/scope caps, and readback agrees at both ends.

### 8.8 Archive scopes: own history, room log, cross-agent audit (R31-023, D-026/D-027)
Archive access is a distinct resource family with its own grants, not a wider `room.read`. Three scopes exist:
| Scope | Contents | Selector | Typical holder | |---|---|---|---| | `own_history` | the caller's own current and prior sessions (live and archived) | `{agents: [self]}` | every agent (granted by default) | | `room_log` | messages/reports in rooms the caller may read, including archived references | `{rooms: [...]}` | room members | | `cross_agent_archive` | another named agent's exported sessions in the archive namespace | `{agents, profiles?, sessions?, threads?, max_checkpoint?}` | auditor supervisors, explicitly granted |
- **VOLC-070 (independent grant of access).** The right to **read** an archive and the right to **grant** archive access are separate records. A manager may grant `cross_agent_archive` only if it holds `grant_use` (or `meta_grant`) for `archive.read` over the target agent's storage; the manager role alone confers nothing (D-026). The grant names: target agent/profile, allowed sessions or threads (or `all_sessions_of_agent`), `max_checkpoint_seq` (a read ceiling), expiry, and whether sub-delegation is permitted. VP configuration bounds the maximum scope; a grant exceeding it is refused `403 grant_outside_pool`. - **VOLC-071 (authorization on every read).** Archive reads are paginated keyset reads served by the archive service. Every page re-checks the grant, the expiry and the selector — authorization is never cached across pages. A read outside the grant returns `404 not_found` (same one-code rule). Every read writes an access-audit record `{actor, grant_id, scope, selector, page_cursor, records_read, ts}`; a read without an audit row is a defect. - **VOLC-072 (completeness, freshness, unavailable data).** A response states the archive manifest's `completeness`, `checkpoint_seq` and `covered_through_ts`, so the auditor knows what it did **not** see. Declared gaps are returned as gap records, not omitted silently. When the archive is unavailable the read fails `503 archive_unavailable` — never an empty success, never a fabricated "no records". Revocation is enforced on the next page (and on a new request within the same session); activation is immediate on grant creation. - **VOLC-072a (audit assignment/result flow).** An audit is a normal assignment: the manager creates a ticket/assignment whose criteria name the target archives the questions to answer; the auditor reads centrally (no source-host login, no host credential), and its report cites exact archive keys + revision/checkpoint for every finding. The report returns through the owning subthread (VOLB-065). The manager's acceptance review checks each citation resolves (existence and revision are machine-checkable), not that the prose is agreeable. - **VOLC-072b (the one named exception to snapshot-stable authority).** Archive reads are the single exception to §8.9 VOLC-069: a session snapshot does NOT extend an archive-read grant past its revocation, expiry or selector narrowing, because the archive spans other agents' sessions and the read itself is paginated verification work. Every page is authorized against **current** grant records (`session_policy.archive_grant_evaluation: "per_page_current"` in `contracts/config.schema.json`); a grant revoked after page N denies page N+1 with `403 tool_not_granted`, cause `revoked`, and the denial is audited with the grant id and page cursor. Use of ordinary (non-archive) capabilities in the same session continues under R7 unchanged. A session holding **no** archive grant — including a session whose only archive access came from a scope that was withdrawn before the session began — is denied `404 not_found` per the single public error contract (§3.6), never an empty page. - **VOLC-072c (why this is safe to make an exception).** The exception is bounded on the other side by the snapshot: the archive grant's *scope* (agents, selectors, `max_checkpoint_seq`) is frozen at session start, so a per-page re-check can only ever narrow what the session was allowed to read, never widen it. Residual-risk note: the asymmetry is deliberate and stated (freshness of authorization over stability of authorization); no other capability family may adopt it without a new decision. - **VOLC-081 (grant record ownership — no implicit read).** The three scopes above are the ONLY archive read scopes; each is held by an explicit GrantRecord (`capability.archive.read`, `resource_scope.archive_scopes`, VOL-B §3.13). Even `own_history` is a granted default, not an inferred right: it exists because VP configuration grants it, and it can be withheld. There is **no implicit read** — no role, membership, or config block alone confers archive access (the `archive` config block bounds the max grantable scopes; it grants nothing). The grant-record schema and the selector grammar for archive scopes (including the QA-1..QA-5 query selectors, VOL-B §5.10) are owned by **CHD31-06**; archive read MUST NOT ship ahead of that record.

### 8.9 Session policy enforcement, fork modes, and resync (R31-027, D-033, D-038)
This section uses [snapshot](terminology.md#snapshot) and [resync](terminology.md#resync) with their package definitions; the rules below specify only this service's endpoint inputs, checks, and writes.
**VOLC-069 (enforcement by snapshot).** Every session gets a `SessionPolicySnapshot` at creation (fresh or fork) and uses it for the session's lifetime. Enforcement reads the snapshot; it does not re-resolve grants per call. Snapshot content, lineage and storage are VOL-B §3.11; the operations are:
| Operation | Endpoint / tool | Authority | Effect | |---|---|---|---| | read effective policy | `GET /v1/sessions/{id}/policy`, `chd_whoami` | self, director, VP | snapshot + `policy_rev` + origins + fork mode | | resync | `POST /v1/sessions/{session_id}/policy-resync`, `chd_session_policy_resync` | the agent's own session-policy authority or a `session.policy_resync` grant | new revision, one atomic write | | fork | provisioning (§4.1) | assigner | child snapshot per `fork_mode` |
**Fork modes (default and alternate).** `session.fork_policy: "preserve_parent_snapshot" | "current_policy"`, default `preserve_parent_snapshot`, scope = global with per-agent override; a per-project override may narrow but never widen the VP setting. Activation is at fork creation and at explicit resync; **never retroactive** to existing sessions. A fork copies `grants`, effective `policy_rev`, `policy_snapshot_id`, each grant's provenance and lineage (`origin`, `grant_id`, `authority_ref`/`ancestors`), and expiry values; it also records `parent_session_id`, `parent_bond_id`, `fork_mode`, and `fork_point_seq`.
| Fork mode | After a parent grant is revoked before the fork | Independent VP-configured grant | Child revision/readback | |---|---|---|---| | `preserve_parent_snapshot` (default) | **Keeps** the revoked-derived grant copied from the parent snapshot; no re-resolution | **Survives**, with `origin: vp_configured` | Copies parent's effective `policy_rev` and provenance/lineage; readback reports this mode | | `current_policy` | **Drops** the revoked-derived grant by resolving current VP/grant records | **Survives**, with `origin: vp_configured` | Uses current effective revision and current provenance/lineage; readback reports this mode |
- `preserve_parent_snapshot` → the child copies the parent's grants and `policy_rev` verbatim. Rights whose source was revoked after the parent session began remain effective for the child (D-033/D-038 default). This is intentional: a session's authority is what it started with. - `current_policy` → the child resolves grants against current VP configuration and current grant records; rights derived from a revoked ancestor are absent. - A tool call never triggers a refresh under either mode. **Preserve-parent mode never auto-resyncs**: neither a revocation, policy activation, read, write, nor grant issuance may silently invoke resync. Negative case: a post-revocation tool call against an untouched preserve-parent session returns according to its copied snapshot and leaves `policy_rev` unchanged; only the explicit operation below can change it.
**In-flight operation semantics.** At a fork boundary, the parent operation already authorized continues under the parent's snapshot; a child read/write/grant issuance starts only after the child snapshot is atomically written. At explicit resync, a read or write already authorized continues under its prior revision, while the next authorization boundary uses the new revision. A grant issuance already admitted continues only for its current request, but its authority is checked against current revocation/lineage rules; a new issuance after resync uses the new snapshot and may not cite a revoked authority. Policy activation changes the mode for future forks (and future sessions); it does not rewrite an existing snapshot or an in-flight read, write, or grant issuance. Each operation class is therefore snapshot-bound at its authorization boundary, not at an arbitrary later request.
**Resync contract.** Body `{expected_policy_rev, reason, approval_ref?}`. Authorization: the caller must be the session's own session-policy authority or hold an explicit `session.policy_resync` grant from an authority that may resync that agent; the request is VP-bound to the target agent/session, and every allow or denial is audited. Effect: compute current policy, write exactly one new snapshot revision (`policy_rev + 1`), audit `{actor, session, from_rev, to_rev, reason, approval_ref}`, and return the new revision. If `expected_policy_rev` is stale → `409 policy_revision_conflict`, no write. Unauthorized → `403 policy_resync_not_granted`, audited. If `session.resync.enabled` is false, the operation is refused with `403 policy_resync_disabled`, audited, and no snapshot changes. The configured authorization sources are `session_policy_authority` and `session.policy_resync`; any caller must match one and remain VP-bound to the target session. Atomicity: either the new revision is committed and readable, or nothing changed — no partial grant set. Limits: resync can only remove revoked-derived rights or pick up newly granted rights **within the agent's configured use pool**; it can never widen beyond VP configuration.
